newsitem.title: INDIA: India coffee reforms seen encouraging new players.
newsitem.headline: India coffee reforms seen encouraging new players.

text.p: India's decision to abolish a pooling mechanism on coffee will have no immediate impact on the market but could spur the entry of new players, officials and growers said on Monday.
"It is not going to make an earth-shattering impact," Philipose Matthai, chairman of the state-run Coffee Board, told Reuters.
The government on Saturday announced that coffee growers would no longer be required to pool their output for auction by the state-run Coffee Board in the domestic and export markets.
It abolished a quota system under which growers were obliged to sell 30 percent of their output to a state-run pool.
Junior Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah said this had been done to encourage growers to increase production and keep in view the "vibrant international market."
"Basically there will be more players in the domestic market, especially producers," said Anil Bhandari, a leading grower and official of the United Planters Association of Southern India (UPASI).
All coffee grown in India used to be pooled via the Coffee Board, which auctioned supplies for domestic and export markets.
In 1995/96 (April-March) the government exempted from the system small growers owning less than 10 hectares of coffee. This accounted for 98 percent of producers.

The remaining two percent, who owned plantation exceeding 10 hectares and accounted for 40 percent of total production, were required to pool 30 percent of their coffee with the board. They were permitted to sell the balance in the open market.
Coffee growers had urged the government to change the 50-year-old law authorising the Coffee Board to handle most coffee marketing activity.
Bhandari said there would be significant reductions in domestic prices, though not immediately, since middlemen would be eliminated from the trade.
He expected exports to remain the same.
In 1995/96 (July-June) India produced 223,000 tonnes of coffee against a target of 200,000. It is expected to produce 219,740 tonnes in 1996/97.
In fiscal 1995/96 (April-March), India exported 168,000 tonnes of coffee worth $430 million compared to 137,395 tonnes worth $350 million 1994/95.

Bhandari said the aim would be to tap the the 300-million strong middle class in the northern and eastern parts of the country. At present barely 50 million people in India are regular coffee drinkers.
"We would wait and see. The idea is to keep the market free, Matthai said. "If the domestic market shoots up then government will intervene."
